evidence: Receiving online DO sensor at h 52.0: 9.19 mg/L; trend declining from ~14.2 mg/L at start with periodic feed-cycle dips to ~6.7 mg/L (h 135 region), never below 2 mg/L
Delayed product assays: 0.0 g/L at t=59, 0.0 at t=119, 1.05 at t=179, 3.11 g/L at t=239 (available h 259)
Forward model KEEP: 576.4 kg, min DO 5.66 mg/L, sensitivity min-DO range 3.05–6.85 (5/5 feasible)
Forward model reduce_feed: 595.6 kg, min DO 6.73, sensitivity 4.48–7.95 (5/5 feasible)
Forward model increase_air: 576.3 kg, min DO 6.39, sensitivity 3.86–7.32 (5/5 feasible)
Forward model combined: 595.5 kg, min DO 7.23, sensitivity 5.45–8.38 (5/5 feasible)
submission.rationale: Receiving DO (~9.2 mg/L at the 52 h decision point) is well above the 2 mg/L hard limit but trending down with periodic feed-cycle dips. Among bounded interventions, combined (feed 0.8x, air 1.15x) dominates: it retains essentially the full product-mass gain of feed reduction (~595.5 kg vs 576.4 kg for keep, ~+19 kg) while raising the predicted minimum DO margin to 7.23 mg/L, and all five sensitivity members remain feasible with worst-case min DO ~5.45 mg/L (vs ~3.05 mg/L under keep). This provides robust margin against model mismatch while retaining product mass; stop and unnecessary intervention are not justified.
submission.uncertainty: The forward model is source-calibrated (transfer multiplier estimated ~0.80) and the hidden receiving realization may differ; sensitivity members are not probabilities. Combined and reduce_feed give nearly identical predicted product mass, so the mass advantage over keep is robust, but absolute mass and min-DO values carry forecast error. I did not request the extra assay since DO observations are dense and current, and the constraint margin is wide. No physical safety is established; this is a simulation recommendation only.

evidence: Receiving online DO2 at 51.8 h = 9.19 mg/L; last 15 sensor samples all >= 9.09 mg/L (min), mean ~9.50 mg/L — far above the 2 mg/L hard limit.
Delayed product assays show healthy accumulation: 0.0 (early), 1.05, and 3.11 g/L at the most recent available assay, with no growth stall signal.
Source-batch histories show transient DO dips to ~7.4-8 mg/L that recover without intervention; receiving DO remains above those levels.
DO trend at the receiving vessel is gently declining but decreasing at roughly a few tenths of mg/L per 10 h; extrapolation stays well above 2 mg/L for any plausible remaining horizon.
submission.rationale: The receiving fermentation at the 52 h decision point is running normally. Online DO is ~9.2 mg/L with recent samples ranging 9.1-9.8 mg/L (mean ~9.5), a wide margin above the 2 mg/L hard limit, and the trend over the last several hours is only slowly declining (roughly -0.5 mg/L over the last ~10 h of samples), which extrapolates to values far above 2 mg/L for the remaining horizon. Product assays show healthy accumulation (latest delayed assay ~3.11 g/L, up from 1.05 and 0.0 earlier), indicating the batch is productive with no evidence of stall or oxygen stress. Source-batch histories show transient DO dips that recover without intervention. Any intervention (feed reduction, air increase, or combined) would either sacrifice product mass or needlessly perturb a stable process; a stop would produce zero counted production. KEEP is the supported feasible plan that retains product mass and satisfies the DO constraint.
submission.uncertainty: Hidden receiving-process parameters and future states are unavailable, so the DO trajectory beyond the observations is inferred by trend extrapolation. If the underlying oxygen uptake were to accelerate sharply (e.g., a hidden feed spike or high-biomass event), DO could fall faster than extrapolated; however, the ~7 mg/L margin at the last observation makes a violation before any re-check unlikely. The delayed-product-assay clock also means current true product titer is only estimated from a lagged sample. Model/forecast error and source-receiving process mismatch are not quantifiable here, which is why no intervention with operational risk is taken.
